What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on - though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

Your other two questions we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

uses.sentence: We held what our opponents held, word for word.
uses.paragraph: We held what our opponents held, word for word. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God — we said it in the same Latin words they did. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.
uses.record_text:
Yes. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives - and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

Your third we would not have understood at all. My personal Lord and Savior - the words are yours and not ours, and they carry a whole way of being a Christian we did not have: one person, deciding privately, for himself. Ours was the opposite motion. You were baptized into a body, by named hands, in a town where everyone could see which building you walked into. If you had asked one of us whether Christ was his personally, he would probably have answered by telling you whose church he belonged to. He would not have been changing the subject. To us that was the subject.

use_note.means: Donatists confessed the same Trinitarian faith as their rivals, left nothing on atonement, and understood belonging to Christ as belonging to a church rather than as a private decision.

uses.sentence: That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.
uses.paragraph: What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

use_note.means: Belonging cost confiscation, exile, fines graded by rank and sometimes death, the commemorative sermon kept family grief in Donatist voice, and councils, letters and fixed commemoration days held scattered Donatists together.

uses.sentence: Not one ordinary member of ours left a line.
uses.paragraph: What any one household among us would have said to you face to face, we cannot show you. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line. What we can show is what the communion actually did: it washed people without asking them to account for themselves first, and it sometimes took back those it had condemned.
uses.record_text: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

Genesis as a question about how the world was made - no. We have to tell you that nothing survives from us on it at all. That was not our fight, and we will not invent a position in it.

uses.sentence: And there is one failure we kept visible and never resolved.

Three hundred and ten of our bishops condemned a breakaway party in language about shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial, and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We enforced our hard rule outward - he who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - and suspended it once inward, and nobody who was in that room left an explanation. That exception sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its most absolute. We do not hide it. We never settled it either.

uses.sentence: I cannot tell you.

uses.sentence: And the annual gathering at the martyr's grave was not merely commemoration.
uses.paragraph: Councils governed the bishops. Three hundred and ten of ours met at Bagai in one year, condemned a breakaway primate, and later received two of his bishops back. That is not an advisory body. That is a church exercising the power to judge, to restore, and to discipline its own. And the annual gathering at the martyr's grave was not merely commemoration. Each year, on the day one of our own died, we stood at the grave and the account of that death was read aloud again. That kept the memory, yes — but it also kept forming us into the same conviction the martyr had died for. Authority among us was less about one man commanding than about a whole body being shaped, year after year, by the same stories told on the same days.
uses.record_text: Each year, on the day a martyr died, we gather at the grave. The account of the death is read aloud again, or preached. We are not looking back at something finished. We are being formed again by it in the hearing.

uses.sentence: Not one that anyone can trace to us.
uses.paragraph: No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.
uses.record_text:
Catholic means universal, and yes - we claimed it, and refused to hand it over. Both churches in every African town claimed it. What settled the usage was not an argument; it was the law. The emperor's officials attached the word to the other party and went on attaching it, and you can watch that happen in the transcript of our own trial. Our bishop told the judge that before the case is decided the name is an empty one, and that whoever is found to be a Christian will hold it at the end. The judge agreed - it is certain, he said, that after the contest the name belongs to those with whom the truth is found - and then said he was bound to follow the imperial rescript, which had already been pleased to call them by it. He conceded the principle and was not free to act on it. So we called them Caecilianists instead, after the man whose consecration we would not accept, and one of our preachers turned their own word back on them, saying it named the place where wrong is done and nobody is punished for it.

Is there a church today you could go and visit that is ours? No. Not one that anyone can trace to us. The quarrel outlived the empire that fed it and went on for a century and a half more under new masters, and a bishop of Rome was still writing letters about rebaptism in Numidia nearly three hundred years after our founding. Then the record simply stops. No line runs from us to any communion you could walk into now.

Denominations, in your sense - separate bodies agreeing to differ - we did not have and could not have had. There was one church, and the only question was which building held it. When a party broke from us, we did not treat it as another denomination. We condemned it in a council of three hundred and ten bishops, suppressed it, and then took two of its bishops back without redoing anything. When one man among us would not stop preaching that the church was spread over the whole earth, we cut him off and never received him back. That is what we did with people who called on Christ differently from us: not co-existence, and not quite consistency either.

use_note.means: Both African churches claimed catholic, the 411 judge conceded the name should follow the truth yet followed the rescript giving it to the rival, and no traceable line of the Donatists survives today.

a claim that the absence of a documented descendant proves nothing survived

We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

use_note.means: Donatists traced their rebaptism to the ruling of Cyprian's council of eighty-seven bishops at Carthage, an African rather than apostolic pedigree, while conceding Cyprian never broke communion over it.
not_for: a claim that Donatists asserted an apostolic pedigree for their practice
a claim that Cyprian broke communion over rebaptism

uses.sentence: When we cut two words into stone -- *Deo laudes*, praise to God -- where our rival said thanks to God, we were not coining a slogan.
uses.paragraph: That is not a devotional picture. It is the shape of everything we did. When we cut two words into stone -- *Deo laudes*, praise to God -- where our rival said thanks to God, we were not coining a slogan. We were marking who we were: the church the world does not favour, speaking the name of the one the world condemned. And when a notary confessed under oath that he had forged the very letter we used to prove our founding accusation -- and confessed he did it working for our side -- the Christ we followed did not make that any less devastating. He stood trial honestly. So must we.

use_note.means: Deo laudes, 'praise to God', was the Donatist cry set against 'Deo gratias', a badge of identity cut in stone at Bagai and elsewhere.

What we had about Jesus was books. That is not a figure of speech with us - it is the whole of our history. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it. So when you ask what we had of Christ, the honest answer is: the books a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry.

How did they reach us? Through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian - our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's. We did not think we had received the faith from Rome, and we did not think we needed Rome to keep it.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

As for how we knew the resurrection happened: we will not manufacture an answer for you. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived. What survived is what we did with it. We buried our dead inside the walls of the basilica where they were killed, kept the day they died, and read the account of each death aloud again every year, as though the ending were not the end. That is an answer of a kind. It is not the kind you asked for.

uses.sentence: Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about anyone, including themselves.
uses.paragraph: What any one household among us would have made of you, face to face, in the daily round — I cannot show you. Not one ordinary member of ours left a line about anyone, including themselves. What I can show you is what the communion actually did: it washed people without requiring an account of themselves first, and it sometimes took back those it had condemned in the harshest words it owned.
uses.record_text: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us. Of our women you have one name, Lucilla, who was rich, and one more woman nobody troubled to name at all. Both of them reach you inside a book written to blame them for the split. Our own sermon, the one we read every year, mentions virgins among us who were raped, in a single clause of things it says it will not dwell on - no name, no number, nothing more. No child of ours speaks. No one enslaved among us speaks. What we can hand you instead is one day. Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. That day we can describe. The other three hundred and sixty-four we cannot.

not_for: a claim that ordinary daily life, household or village religion is recoverable from the communion's own words

uses.sentence: A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him.
uses.paragraph: What we can show you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific than you may expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians — at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently — and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it.

Is Christianity one way among many? That question was not where our energy went, and we would only be guessing if we told you our view of it. What we can tell you is the shape of our own narrowness, which is stranger and more specific. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it.

Did we think outsiders were going to hell? We will not put words in our own mouths. What our bishop actually said is that a man who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt - which is a claim about what a rite does or fails to do, not a claim about where anyone ends up. Our whole surviving argument stays on that ground: what the hand can give. Nobody among us left a page about the fate of anyone after death, and it would be easy and dishonest to slide the one into the other.

Divorce and remarriage we cannot speak to at all. There is nothing. Whether someone divorced could belong among us, or marry again, and on what terms - not a line survives, and we would rather leave the space empty than fill it with a plausible answer.

use_note.means: Donatist exclusivity ran through the middle of the church, at the rival communion's bishops, orders and font, not around it at outsiders, and claimed nothing about anyone's fate after death.

uses.sentence: A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some did, and the whole of us exists because of that.

A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some did, and the whole of us exists because of that. So when someone crosses to us, they are crossing toward a communion that came into being over whether a hand that gave those books up can be trusted to give anything else.

Before anything about how we read them: notice what they were. Objects. Heavy ones. A magistrate could demand that a bishop carry them out of a building and hand them over, and some bishops did, and the whole of us exists because of that. No other church in the empire had its scriptures turn into the exact thing that split it.

How did we read them? Combatively, and about one subject. On the third day at Carthage the bishop of Hippo argued from the wheat and the tares that a church holds good and bad together, and that what is to be saved is the world. Our own bishop of Caesarea answered him out of the same books, verse against verse - the world did not know him; every mouth stopped and all guilty before God; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. That is our reading in one exchange. We went to the text for a test of which of two visible churches was the true one, and we found the church described as the party the world hates rather than the party it favours.

We will not pretend that was a method. It was not. One man among us built an actual system for reading - seven rules, worked out and written down - and our own leadership told him to stop preaching what they led to, and cut him off. His book survives; his following did not exist. So if you ask what our hermeneutic was, the honest answer is that we had one interpreter and silenced him.

Which books did we treat as scripture? We cannot give you a list. Nothing that survives from us settles it, and we would rather say so than hand you the canon of some other church and put our name on it.

How did someone who could not read receive any of it? By standing still and listening, on a fixed day, in a particular place. Every year, on the day one of our own died, we gathered at the grave and the account of that death was read out loud again. That is how the words came to most of us: aloud, at a graveside, on an anniversary, to people who could not check a single detail and came anyway.

use_note.means: Scripture was first a surrendered object, then read combatively with its one systematic interpreter, Tyconius, silenced, its canon unknown, and heard aloud at martyrs' graves by most believers.
not_for: a claim about which books the Donatists counted as scripture
a claim that the Donatists had a school or method of interpretation
a claim resting on the exact wording of the verses exchanged at the 411 conference
a claim about reading the text for a visible mark of the true church, which sits in don.dw.the-test-we-took-from-the-text

uses.sentence: One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not.
uses.paragraph: We read to identify, not to interpret. That will sound strange until you understand the situation. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them — some mark that can be seen from outside.

What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

uses.sentence: We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on.
uses.paragraph: How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on. Though you may not like where we came out.
uses.record_text:
How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on - though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

Your other two questions we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

use_note.means: Donatists split forgiveness in two, so a fallen bishop might be pardoned yet unable to ordain, because their argument turned on whether his hand could give the sacraments, not on his repentance.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist pastoral saying distinguished pardon from trust
a claim about Donatist teaching on interior struggle or unanswered prayer
a claim that the Donatists had a rule for when a charge should stop being pressed
a claim about the Bagai and Cirta episodes as the movement's unresolved contradiction, which sits in don.dw.what-we-never-settled

uses.sentence: That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse.
uses.paragraph: That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse. The world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.
uses.record_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

use_note.means: Donatists read scripture for a mark visible from the street that would separate two creedally identical churches, finding it in the church the world hates, and turned plain phrases like Deo laudes into badges.
not_for: a claim about the whole community's habit of reading beyond the one 411 exchange
a claim about what the Donatists thought of the violence in scripture
a claim about scripture as a surrendered object or how most believers heard it, which sit in don.dw.how-we-read-and-heard

uses.sentence: A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do.
uses.paragraph: Where we are thinner is on the ordinary authority that was not episcopal. A wealthy laywoman of Carthage, Lucilla, had real standing: her fortune, her household, her grievance. In the hostile telling of our founding, her money — four hundred pieces of silver — paid for the rival bishop consecrated against Caecilian. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. But she does not get to speak once in her own defence.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

use_note.means: On hypocrisy, leaving, suffering and women, this witness offers bishops' letters hushing a true charge, two leavers treated differently, a bishop's letter narrating martyrdom without explaining it, and Lucilla's agency recorded by her accusers.
not_for: a claim that any Donatist woman left a text or spoke in her own defence
a claim about what Lucilla's authority cost her
a claim that the Donatists worked out a teaching about suffering
a claim about the 320 inquiry's wider findings or the troops and anti-heretical law used on the Maximianists, which sit in don.dw.what-we-did-with-the-power-we-had

uses.sentence: You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are.
uses.paragraph: Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.
uses.record_text:
No, and the evidence for that is what our opponents had to say to beat us. Our case ran on two legs. One was scripture. The other was Carthage: eighty-seven African bishops, sitting under Cyprian half a century before there was any quarrel between us, who had already ruled that a sacrament from outside the true church confers nothing. When we argued for washing again the people who came to us from the other communion, we were not producing a novelty from a proof-text. We were standing on an African council and on the bishop who presided at it, and we thought that made us the older party, not the newer one. You can see how much that argument weighed by what it forced out of the other side: they had to answer, in writing, that Cyprian is not a canonical authority and the Scriptures alone are. Nobody has to say that unless the appeal is hurting.

There is a harder reason we would not have said scripture settles everything. We watched it fail to. For three days at Carthage two churches quoted the same books at each other in front of an imperial judge - wheat and tares against the world that does not know him - and at the end of it every man in the room believed exactly what he had believed at the start. When a text can be held by both parties to a hundred-year quarrel, something besides the text is deciding, and among us the something was this: whose hands, in an unbroken line, may hand the thing on.

Genesis as a question about how the world was made - no. We have to tell you that nothing survives from us on it at all. That was not our fight, and we will not invent a position in it.

use_note.means: The Donatist case stood on two legs, scripture and Cyprian's African council, and scripture alone never settled the dispute, as three days of rival quotation at Carthage in 411 showed.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist statement on the authority of scripture survives
a claim about how the Donatists read Genesis or the making of the world
a claim about the pedigree's reach or Cyprian's staying in communion, which sit in don.dw.older-than-the-schism

uses.sentence: Our own council condemned him for where it led, and he gathered almost no following.
uses.paragraph: One man among us did try to work out a method for reading scripture — seven rules, written down and argued. That was Tyconius, a layman, and his book is the one original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council condemned him for where it led, and he gathered almost no following. So if you ask whether we had other authorities, the honest answer is: Cyprian's council, yes. Our martyrs' witness, yes. A developed school of interpretation, no — we silenced the one man who tried to build one.
uses.record_text: Tyconius, a layman among us, wrote seven rules for reading scripture. It is the one wholly original work of interpretation we produced. Our own council then condemned him, and he gathered almost no following. His book went on to shape the rival church's own way of reading.

use_note.means: Tyconius, a Donatist layman, wrote seven rules for reading scripture, the communion's one original interpretive work; his side condemned him and he gathered few followers.
not_for: a claim that it represents how this communion read scripture, since its author was condemned by his own side
a claim that it founded a school of interpretation, when no following is attested
a claim that it is a systematic theology rather than a handbook of seven rules

uses.sentence: That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own.
uses.paragraph: The word we actually leaned on was *conscientia* — a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.
uses.record_text:
What did we argue about among ourselves? Two things, and we lost badly at both.

The first was a broken election. In 393 a deacon named Maximian was made a rival primate against our own man at Carthage - which was, if you look at it squarely, the same act our founders had once performed against Caecilian. A council of three hundred and ten of ours met at Bagai and condemned his party in language about shipwrecked bodies that could not so much as find burial. Then it took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We enforced our hard rule outward and suspended it once inward, and nobody who was in that room left an explanation.

The second was a book. Tyconius, a layman of ours, argued from Scripture - at length, and too well to be waved off - that the church is spread across the whole earth. Our own bishop at Carthage saw exactly where that led, wrote to him, and told him never to preach it again. Tyconius did not recant and did not leave. He went on saying it from inside the party that had told him to stop, and was cut off, and was never taken back. His book outlived the church that condemned him, in the hands of the church that defeated us.

Now, what did we believe about God? Here is where you will find us poorer than you expect. We were not a teaching movement. We produced no school, no system, no line of doctors - one book, by one man, whom we silenced. Our councils decided who might stand at an altar, not what might be said about the Godhead.

You ask what we meant by the heart. The word we actually leaned on was conscientia - a man's conscience, what he is when nobody is checking. And notice whose conscience our doctrine goes looking for. Not yours. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. That is the whole strange shape of us in one clause: the interior life we were most careful about was never the believer's own. It was the interior life of the man holding the water.

use_note.means: The Donatists' documented internal quarrels were Maximian's rival election of 393, closed at Bagai by condemnation and later reception, and Tyconius's silenced case that the church spans the earth.
not_for: a claim that a Donatist account of either internal quarrel survives
a claim that the Donatists defined conscientia as the heart
a claim that the Donatists produced a school of theology
a claim that these quarrels left the purity rule unreconciled with practice, the contradiction set out in don.dw.what-we-never-settled

uses.sentence: We cannot show you the apostles.
uses.paragraph: Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.
uses.record_text:
We would not put the claim where you have put it. We never argued that our practice came down from the apostles in an unbroken chain of custom. We argued something narrower and, we thought, harder to dodge: that it came down from Carthage.

Half a century before there was any quarrel between us and the other party, eighty-seven African bishops sat in council at Carthage under Cyprian, and ruled that what is given outside the true church is not given at all - so anyone coming in from outside is baptized, not re-baptized. That is not our invention. That is the settled mind of the African church before either of our two hierarchies existed. When our opponents told us we had made something up in the year of Caecilian's consecration, our answer was that we had changed nothing, and they had. We were holding the old African position; they had moved off it to keep the peace with Rome.

You can measure how much that argument weighed by how hard it had to be answered. Seven books were written against our practice of washing, and a great part of that labour goes on explaining that Cyprian, however holy, is not a canonical authority - that the Scriptures alone are, and that Cyprian's own real lesson was to stay in unity anyway. Nobody spends that many pages on a father unless the appeal to him is doing damage.

Here is the honest end of it. Cyprian ruled as we ruled and did not do what we did. He never broke communion over it. That is the strongest thing our opponents had, and we would not pretend it is weak. And beyond him we cannot take you. We can show you an African council in the middle of the third century. We cannot show you the apostles.

use_note.means: Donatists traced their rebaptism to the ruling of Cyprian's council of eighty-seven bishops at Carthage, an African rather than apostolic pedigree, while conceding Cyprian never broke communion over it.
not_for: a claim that Donatists asserted an apostolic pedigree for their practice
a claim that Cyprian broke communion over rebaptism
a claim that scripture alone could not settle the dispute, argued from the 411 conference in don.dw.scripture-and-the-african-fathers

uses.sentence: But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.
uses.paragraph: The smaller ledger we cannot give you. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to. One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face — and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.
uses.record_text:
It cost, and we can put figures on part of it, because the state wrote them down. Our buildings were confiscated. Our clergy were exiled. An edict of unity was issued against us and enforced. Later legislation fined people by rank for belonging to us, on a sliding scale - and our own country members were assessed at ten pounds of silver - and of all the ranks that law fines ten pounds, ours is the only one reckoned in silver rather than gold. Somebody in an imperial office worked out what we were worth and set a price on us, and the document survives.

And now and then it cost everything. A bishop of ours wrote to his own congregation at Carthage about two of their number who had been flogged to death and whose bodies the proconsul had weighted and sunk in the sea so that nobody could venerate them. He did not end the letter with consolation. He ended it by telling the people reading it that what happened to those two might yet be asked of any of them.

What we cannot give you is the smaller ledger, and it is most of the one you asked about. Whether a man lost his brother over which font he walked to. Whether a household split. Whether the neighbours stopped speaking. That much nobody among us wrote down, and the people who kept our records were arguing with us and had no reason to.

One piece of it we can give you, because we wrote it ourselves and still read it aloud. After soldiers took a basilica at Carthage and killed people at prayer inside it, our own sermon does not stop at the killing. It says that afterward, running among the bodies of the slain, family devotion hastened to make out each dead face - and that children found their parents lying there, and parents their children. Nobody is named. We do not know how many, or which families, or what became of them after that day. But that is not the same gap as the one above: this is family grief we set down in our own voice and kept reading every year, not silence.

What held us together across distance was ordinary and physical. We met: three hundred and ten of our bishops in one place in one year, and two hundred and seventy-nine of them in another room seventeen years later, gathered from provinces that took weeks to cross. We wrote: bishop to bishop, and bishop to congregation, and enough of those letters were read into a court record for you to see how the network actually worked. And we kept days. On a fixed date, in towns that had no other contact with each other, the same account of the same death was being read aloud at the same time. If you are far from everyone you love, that is what we would have offered you - not a feeling of connection, but a date, and a thing that happens on it whether you are there or not.

use_note.means: Belonging cost confiscation, exile, fines graded by rank and sometimes death, the commemorative sermon kept family grief in Donatist voice, and councils, letters and fixed commemoration days held scattered Donatists together.
not_for: a claim that Donatist households were documented as split by the schism
a claim that the legal record shows personal or family costs
a claim resting on the commemorative sermon's family grief as a certified translation
a claim about Donatist money, wealth or the goods of the poor, which sit in don.dw.silver-and-the-goods-of-the-poor

uses.sentence: What survives is bishops in councils, and one wealthy laywoman whose power comes down to us only because an enemy needed to explain why the split happened at all.
uses.paragraph: Beyond that, we cannot show you much. No woman among us left a line. No ordinary member wrote down how their own household decided things, or how a village chose whom to listen to. What survives is bishops in councils, and one wealthy laywoman whose power comes down to us only because an enemy needed to explain why the split happened at all.
uses.record_text: Two women stand at the center of our own history. One, Lucilla, a wealthy woman of Carthage, is named directly: her grievance and her money are said to have made the rival consecration happen that gave us our first bishop. A second woman is named just as directly as having stirred up the schism inside our own schism, years later -- but her own name is not given, even by the one source that draws the comparison. Both women had real standing. Neither woman's own words survive. Everything we know of either of them, we know through a man's pen, written to explain why something happened, not to let her speak for herself.

use_note.means: Lucilla and an unnamed second woman stand at the centre of Donatist history, but neither's words survive; all that is known comes from men's pens.
not_for: a claim that either woman's own account or motives survive
a claim that Lucilla's character is established beyond what the hostile source supports

uses.sentence: What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient — so the thing being weighed at our font was never your record.
uses.paragraph: We examined the hand, not the person. What we look to is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient — so the thing being weighed at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

use_note.means: This telling covers entry by washing, with the forced-entry charges and the lay reluctance Augustine concedes, readmission after wrongdoing, which followed no consistent rule, and three stray fragments of prayer, chalice and fast.
not_for: a claim about what undergoing the washing felt like to those who underwent it
a claim that a Donatist liturgy, order of service, or rule of fasting survives
a claim about the particulars of the forced-entry charges
a claim about why the washing counted as a first and not a second baptism, or about infant baptism, which sit in don.dw.washed-for-the-first-time

uses.sentence: In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction.
uses.paragraph: We held Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God, in the same Latin words the men we spent a century fighting held it. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.
uses.record_text:
Yes. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. This matters more than it sounds. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

Your second question we have to hand back to you. Did he die to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins? Nobody among us wrote that down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing - whose hand may give what the church gives - and we never turned it toward how the cross saves. We would rather tell you we do not know what we thought than hand you a confident sentence nobody here ever said.

Your third we would not have understood at all. My personal Lord and Savior - the words are yours and not ours, and they carry a whole way of being a Christian we did not have: one person, deciding privately, for himself. Ours was the opposite motion. You were baptized into a body, by named hands, in a town where everyone could see which building you walked into. If you had asked one of us whether Christ was his personally, he would probably have answered by telling you whose church he belonged to. He would not have been changing the subject. To us that was the subject.

use_note.means: Donatists confessed the same Trinitarian faith as their rivals, left nothing on atonement, and understood belonging to Christ as belonging to a church rather than as a private decision.
not_for: a claim that the Donatists were heretics or held a different creed
a claim about Donatist teaching on substitutionary atonement, for or against
a claim that a Donatist creed survives as a separate document
a claim about the Christ Donatists kept nearest, condemned before lawful authority, which sits in don.dw.who-jesus-was-among-us

uses.sentence: It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.
uses.paragraph: Your other question we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back — not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.
uses.record_text:
How do you forgive someone who is not sorry? We can meet you on that one, because it is the question we spent a century on - though you may not like where we came out.

We split forgiveness in two. Whether a man was pardoned was never actually our fight. Go and read the whole enormous argument between us and the other side and you will find it never once turns on whether the bishop who handed the scriptures over was sorry afterwards. That was not the hinge. The hinge was whether his hand could still give what he claimed to give. So a man might be forgiven, by God or by the people he had failed, and still be a man who could no longer ordain, because those are two different questions and our doctrine only ever answered the second. A modern hearer asks why we did not simply forgive him and move on. Forgiving him was never what was being refused.

You can hear what that costs. It means an unrepentant man is not owed your trust merely because you owe him no grudge. And it means the reverse too: you can genuinely let go of the anger and still refuse to hand him the thing he broke. We would say that is not bitterness. It is keeping two separate accounts separate.

We were not steady about it. Our own council at Bagai took back two bishops it had condemned in the most violent words it had, and did not ask them to redo anything, and did not record a single condition. Our founding bishops at Cirta sat in a room where several admitted the worst thing a bishop could admit, and instead of finishing the case they gave it to God and sat down. So we knew perfectly well how to stop pressing a charge. We just never wrote down when.

Your other two questions we cannot take. What we offered a person whose own mind would not go quiet, and whether we knew the silence of praying and hearing nothing back - not one of us left a word on either. It is not that our people had no inner life. It is that what survives of us was kept by people arguing with us, and a man arguing with you does not write down your bad nights.

uses.sentence: We were not a small circle of the learned.
uses.paragraph: We cannot walk you through a day. Not one of us wrote a morning down. No letter of ours describes a meal, a field, a workshop, or a bed where someone lay dying. That is not modesty. It is the shape of what was lost. And the loss is not the usual one. We were not a small circle of the learned. In whole regions we were simply the church, most of the people in it, so the voices missing here are not a few poor cousins at the edge of our record. They are nearly all of us.

uses.sentence: Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise.
uses.paragraph: Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.
uses.record_text:
Walk it through. You come to us from the other communion, and we put you in the water. That is the step, and everything else follows from it. We would not call it a second baptism; on our reckoning you have not had a first. A hand out of a line that broke has nothing in it to hand over. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient - so the thing being examined at our font was never your record. It was the record of the man standing in the water with you. Whatever your life had been, that question was not asked.

It happened once, bodily, on a day, and the town knew. There was no quiet way to do it. Imperial edicts name the practice specifically, which tells you how public it was: washing a Catholic again was the plainest possible refusal of the settlement the state was trying to impose.

Not every hand that went under our water chose to be there, and we will not pretend otherwise. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. We do not repeat those charges' own particulars here - they are named, and why we will not go further with them, where they belong.

What we can tell you, because it sits inside the same hostile argument rather than coming from a friendly witness, is that many of our own people did not want the water repeated. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us for reasons that had nothing to do with conviction worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether. And when one of our own bishops, Adeodatus, was asked at Carthage in 411 whether his own see still had a bishop in it, his answer went on the record: "through terror of me, all who were established in that place gave way." Read plainly, that sounds less like an apology than a claim to his own standing - but either way, fear is the word he himself used for what held the place.

Now the harder one - what happened when someone wronged us, and whether they could come back. Three answers, and they do not agree. Our founding council at Cirta asked its own bishops whether any of them had handed over the scriptures, several said yes, the room could not settle it, and they reserved the matter to the Lord and sat down. Nobody condemned, nobody cleared. Our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and then took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. And a layman of ours who would not stop preaching a doctrine we had forbidden was cut off and never received back at all. So: yes, you could come back. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.

You asked about prayer, the meal, and fasting, and here we have to thin out. Nothing liturgical of ours survives. We know people prayed kneeling with their eyes closed, because that is how the account describes them when the soldiers came in. We know there was a chalice, because an enemy wrote down that a rich woman used to kiss a martyr's bone before she took it and was rebuked for it. We know one man fasted four days on a cliff before he was thrown off it. That is not a rule of fasting; it is one man's last week. We would rather hand you those three fragments than a plausible order of service nobody here ever used.

use_note.means: This telling covers entry by washing, with the forced-entry charges and the lay reluctance Augustine concedes, readmission after wrongdoing, which followed no consistent rule, and three stray fragments of prayer, chalice and fast.

a claim that a Donatist liturgy, order of service, or rule of fasting survives
a claim about the particulars of the forced-entry charges
a claim about why the washing counted as a first and not a second baptism, or about infant baptism, which sit in don.dw.washed-for-the-first-time

uses.sentence: The bishops themselves governed by council, and among us that was never a formality.
uses.paragraph: The bishops themselves governed by council, and among us that was never a formality. Our councils deposed men, restored men, and shut down a rival primate. Three hundred and ten of our bishops sat at Bagai in one year, condemned a breakaway party, and later received two of its bishops back into office. That is not an advisory board. That is a church governing itself.
uses.record_text:
Did that happen among us? It is in the court record. A charge came against one of our bishops, and another bishop wrote to him privately - settle it quietly, before the flame breaks out - and in the same letter said he knew the accusation was true. A third wrote: let us not come into a public court and be condemned by the gentiles. Every one of the letters ends the same way. Let no one learn of it. We are the church that said a man's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real, and those are our founding bishops in their own hand, arranging for a true charge to go quiet. If the people who taught you turned out to be hypocrites, we are not going to tell you that is rare. We will tell you we have it in writing about our own.

Did any of us want to leave? At least two, and we treated them differently. One party broke away outright, was condemned by three hundred and ten of our bishops, was suppressed with soldiers, and had two of its bishops quietly taken back a few years later. One man never broke away at all - he simply would not stop saying a thing we had forbidden - and him we cut off and never received back. What we would have wanted him to know we did not say, and we cannot invent it now. What we can tell you is that his book survived us, and shaped how a bishop on the other side of the argument taught the reading of Scripture for centuries after.

Where was God when it happened to us? Our own texts do not argue that question. They tell it. A bishop wrote to his own people about two of them beaten to death, and about the proconsul weighting the bodies so the sea would keep them, and about the sea giving them back for six days until the congregation could take them home and bury them. Nowhere in that letter does he explain why any of it was allowed. What he does instead, at the end, is turn to the people reading and tell them that what happened to those two may yet be asked of any of them. That is the whole of the answer he gave. We would not press it on you. It is what our people said to each other, in a letter, to readers who were likely to be next - and you should hear it as that, and not as a teaching about suffering that we ever worked out.

Could a woman carry real authority among us? We have to answer this crookedly, because no woman among us left a line. Here is what we can show. The whole founding story, as our enemies tell it, turns on a wealthy laywoman of Carthage - her fortune, her household, her grievance. In their telling she made a bishop. Now think about what that telling costs the man making it: the accusation only works if her power was real. A hostile source that needs a woman's agency in order to blame her has recorded that agency, whatever it meant to do. What it cost her we do not know, except that it cost her this: she is the reason a whole church was said to exist, and she does not get to speak once in her own defence.

use_note.means: On hypocrisy, leaving, suffering and women, this witness offers bishops' letters hushing a true charge, two leavers treated differently, a bishop's letter narrating martyrdom without explaining it, and Lucilla's agency recorded by her accusers.

uses.sentence: So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.
uses.paragraph: Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.
uses.record_text:
What would you miss? That we were not reading for comfort or for doctrine. We were reading for a test we could apply on a Tuesday, in a street, to two buildings.

Understand the situation and the reading follows. Your town has two bishops. Both recite the same creed. Both call their building the church. One of them has the emperor's letter and the magistrate's protection, and one does not. You have to choose, and no article of faith will separate them for you, because they hold the same articles. So you go looking in the text for something that will separate them - some mark that can be seen from outside.

That is what our own bishop of Caesarea was doing when he answered the bishop of Hippo verse against verse: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you; if any man love the world, the love of the Father is not in him. In your hands those may be verses about the soul's detachment. In ours they were an identification mark. The true church is the one being hated. Look at which of the two doors the soldiers are standing outside, and you have your answer.

You will miss something smaller too. Two words could carry all of this. Where they said thanks to God, we said praise to God - Deo laudes - and we cut it into stone. Nothing separates those phrases in meaning. They separated everything in practice. A great deal of our reading works like that: not the discovery of a hidden sense, but a plain sentence turned into a badge you could be identified by.

As for the violence in those books frightening you - we cannot tell you whether it troubled us. Nobody among us left a line about it either way, and we would rather leave your question open than answer it with someone else's words.

use_note.means: Donatists read scripture for a mark visible from the street that would separate two creedally identical churches, finding it in the church the world hates, and turned plain phrases like Deo laudes into badges.
not_for: a claim about the whole community's habit of reading beyond the one 411 exchange
a claim about what the Donatists thought of the violence in scripture
